summary: This standards-track RFC defines the Router Information Link State Advertisement for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, which lets routers advertise optional capabilities to others in the routing domain. Knowing what neighbors and other routers support helps with features that not everyone has.

plainLanguage.summary: Each router can put up a sign listing what extra things it can do, so other routers know whether to ask it for those things.

questions: what is the ospf router information lsa
what is the ospf router functional capabilities tlv
subtitle: A single OSPF advertisement where routers list the optional features they support.

tldr.problem: Routers in an OSPF domain benefit from knowing what their neighbors and other routers support, but the options field in OSPFv2 has no free bits left for new optional capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The Router Information (RI) LSA carries Type/Length/Value triplets. One TLV lists informational capability bits and another lists functional capability bits, flooded at link, area or AS scope.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4970, adding multiple RI LSA instances per router and the Router Functional Capabilities TLV. Future OSPF extensions can use the RI LSA as their only advertisement mechanism.

today: RFC 7770 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 4970. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Routers Advertise Capabilities
sections.content:
It is useful for routers in an OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 routing domain to know the capabilities of their neighbors and of other routers in the domain. OSPF already uses the options field in LSAs and hello packets for this, but in OSPFv2 all the bits in that field have been allocated, so no new optional capabilities can be added there.

This RFC fills the gap with a new Router Information (RI) LSA. In OSPFv2 it is an Opaque LSA; in OSPFv3 it is an LSA with its own type. For capabilities that already exist, backwards compatibility means the RI LSA is used mainly for information. For future extensions it MAY be the only advertisement and discovery mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The old sign had no room left for new items. So routers get a new, bigger sign that can list anything new.

sections.title: The RI LSA in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3
sections.content:
In OSPFv2 the RI LSA is an Opaque LSA with Opaque type 4. The Opaque ID is the instance ID, and the first instance is always 0. It can be link-scoped (LSA type 9), area-scoped (type 10) or AS-scoped (type 11).

In OSPFv3 the RI LSA has function code 12. The S1 and S2 bits of the LSA type give the flooding scope, and the U bit is set so the LSA is flooded even by routers that do not understand it. The Link State ID is the instance ID, and a router MAY advertise multiple RI LSAs per flooding scope.

In both protocols, instance 0 SHOULD always carry the Router Informational Capabilities TLV and, if advertised, the Router Functional Capabilities TLV. Later instances hold information that does not fit in the first.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router can post several notes. The first note always holds the main list, and extra notes hold whatever did not fit.

sections.title: TLV Format
sections.content:
The body of an RI LSA is a series of nested Type/Length/Value (TLV) triplets, in the same format as the Traffic Engineering extensions to OSPF. Type and Length are each 16 bits. Length counts only the value, in octets.

Each TLV is padded to 4-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in Length. A 3-octet value has Length 3 but occupies 8 octets in total, and a 1-octet value gets 3 octets of padding. Padding is made of undefined bits. Receivers ignore unrecognized types. Any specification that defines a new RI TLV MUST say whether it applies to OSPFv2 only, OSPFv3 only, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each item on the sign has a label, a length and the contents. Items are padded so they all line up neatly, and a router skips any label it does not know.

sections.title: Informational and Functional Capabilities
sections.content:
The Router Informational Capabilities TLV (type 1) is optional. If present, it MUST be the first TLV in instance 0 and MUST accurately reflect the router's capabilities in the advertised scope. These bits have no effect on OSPF operation. Initially the Length is 4, meaning 4 octets of capability bits, numbered from the most significant bit as bit 0.

The assigned bits are 0 (graceful restart capable), 1 (graceful restart helper), 2 (stub router support), 3 (traffic engineering support), 4 (point-to-point over LAN) and 5 (experimental TE). Bits 6 to 31 are unassigned.

The new Router Functional Capabilities TLV (type 2) is also optional and goes in instance 0. Unlike the informational TLV, it MUST reflect the router's actual capabilities because other routers MAY use it to dictate protocol operation. If the TLV is absent, or its length does not cover an assigned bit, that capability is implicitly advertised as not supported. Specifications of functional capabilities MUST describe protocol behavior and address backwards compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: One list is just for information, like a poster of hobbies. The other list is a promise that other routers may rely on, so it has to be true.

sections.title: Flooding Scope
sections.content:
The flooding scope of an RI LSA is set by the LSA type. For OSPFv2, a type 9, 10 or 11 Opaque LSA may be flooded. For OSPFv3 the S1 and S2 bits decide. The choice is made by the advertising router as a matter of local policy.

If AS-wide scope is chosen, the originating router should also advertise area-scoped LSAs into any attached Not-So-Stubby Area (NSSA). A router MAY advertise different capabilities in the NSSA area-scoped LSAs and the AS-scoped LSA. That lets functional capabilities be limited in scope; the RFC's example is an area border router that supports traffic engineering in only some of its attached areas.

A router MAY advertise multiple RI LSAs with the same instance ID as long as their flooding scopes differ. Flooding-scope rules for each TLV must be given in the specification that defines it.
sections.plainLanguage: A router decides how far its sign is shown: just the next-door link, one neighborhood, or the whole town.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
Router Information TLVs that were already being advertised SHOULD continue to be advertised in instance 0. If the same TLV appears in several instances and the RFC defining that TLV does not say how to process multiple instances, the instance with the numerically smallest instance ID is used and the others are ignored.

Compared with RFC 4970, the main change is support for multiple instances of the RI LSA. The RFC also adds the functional capabilities TLV, moves the IANA policy for several registries from Standards Action to IETF Review, and updates references.
sections.plainLanguage: If the same item shows up on two notes, the router reads the oldest, lowest-numbered note and ignores the rest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC describes a generic mechanism plus two TLVs. It says the capability TLVs are less critical than the topology information the base OSPF protocol already advertises. Security considerations for the generic mechanism depend on future applications and should be described as new capabilities are proposed. Security for base OSPF is covered in RFC 2328 and RFC 5340.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign matters less than the road map, but anyone adding something new to the sign must think about what could go wrong.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
RFC 4970 had already defined the Router Information Opaque LSA as type 4 and created the OSPFv3 LSA Function Codes and RI TLV registries. This RFC updates those references and their definitions. OSPFv3 function code 12 is the RI LSA. RI TLV values 1 and 2 are the two capability TLVs, and values 3 to 9 were already assigned. Function codes 16 to 255 and TLV types 10 to 32767 are unassigned under IETF Review.

IANA also created a new subregistry, OSPF Router Functional Capability Bits, which starts out empty. Additions to both capability-bit registries are by IETF Review.
sections.plainLanguage: A keeper of the official list writes down which label numbers mean what, so nobody reuses the same number for two things.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Identifies the TLV; 1 and 2 are the capability TLVs.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value in octets, not counting padding.

fields.name: Value...
fields.desc: Variable-length value, padded to a 4-octet boundary.

cells: May be used by other routers to dictate protocol operation
